name: Deae Matres
sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Deae Matres are Continental Celtic goddesses. The Latin name translates as "Divine Mothers." They form one of the most common goddess images in Celtic lands. The sculptures sometimes show two mothers, but more often three. Three was the number of intensification to the Celts. The Mothers usually sit, and they often appear as different ages: a young maiden, a fertile mother, and an aging crone. Sometimes they appear as identical triplets. They hold sacred objects: a sacrificial knife, an offering plate or patera, foodstuffs, bread, and fish. These goddesses are tied to the fertility of the land and its people, so they are linked to food and abundance. Besides the figure called Dea Nutrix, the nourishing goddess, the Mothers also appear as a single voluptuous woman holding fertility symbols. This form is called the pseudo-Venus or false Venus. No ritual connected to these goddesses survives in history. They seem to have been absorbed into the Roman religious framework early in imperial times.
objective: The Deae Matres, the Divine Mothers, their triple figure, and their absorption into the Roman religious framework.
key_results: They usually appear as three seated women of different ages.
They hold patera, bread, fish, and other sacred objects.
They were absorbed into Roman religion in early imperial times.
